title: Redwood Private (On-Prem/Air-Gapped) Technical Deep Dive — upgrades, rollback, offline bundles
summary: Enterprise on-prem prospect (air-gapped requirement) asked detailed questions on Redwood Private upgrades/rollback: supported maintenance window patterns, deterministic upgrade ordering, backup/snapshot expectations, downgrade limitations (forward-only DB migrations), and offline artifact delivery (bundle format + signing + verification + key rotation). Redwood walked through the installer-driven upgrade plan, precheck gates (k8s/storage/permissions/disk), backup verification, and operator UX for abort/rollback. Customer emphasized change-control, auditable evidence, and an option to run non-interactively for automation.
topics: Artifact signing, verification, and key custody/rotation
Upgrade sequencing and health gates (control plane → runtime → gateways → observability)
Rollback behavior, rollback windows, and forward-only migrations
Backups: control-plane DB snapshot + restore drill expectations
Maintenance windows, expected downtime, and canary patterns
Operator UX: interactive prompts vs flags; producing evidence for change management
Diagnostics bundle contents for failed upgrades
questions: Can we import an offline bundle and verify it without performing the upgrade (dry run)?
What exactly is the rollback boundary if the database migration has run?
Do you support downgrade across major versions or only patch/minor within a window?
How do you prove to auditors that the artifacts installed match what you shipped (provenance)?
Can the upgrade be run fully non-interactive in our automation (Ansible/Jenkins)?
What is a realistic maintenance window for a 3-node control plane + 8 GPU nodes deployment?
next_steps: Redwood (Bruno) to share offline bundle / signing overview doc + sample manifest fields (hashes, versions, signatures).
Redwood (Connor) to send draft upgrade runbook sections on rollback boundaries and forward-only migration guardrails.
Customer (Dan/Priya) to provide target environment details: k8s version, storage class, snapshot capabilities, and current change window constraints.
Redwood (Marcus Lin) to confirm recommended key custody model (customer-held vs Redwood-held) and key rotation process for air-gapped installs.
Schedule follow-up: 60 min workshop for customer’s internal release/change-management team to walk through an example upgrade evidence packet.
action_items: Owner: Bruno Silva — Send sample offline bundle layout + verification steps (incl. how to run verify-only) — Due: 2025-01-16
Owner: Connor O'Brien — Provide upgrade/rollback ordering diagram + rollback decision table (what is reversible vs not) — Due: 2025-01-17
Owner: Marcus Lin — Answer security questionnaire items: signing keys, rotation cadence, audit log events for upgrade/rollback — Due: 2025-01-17
Owner: Dan Wu — Share AsterPeak’s on-prem cluster constraints (no outbound, internal registry, snapshot permissions) — Due: 2025-01-20
Owner: Markus Klein — Coordinate next workshop invite w/ AsterPeak change-management stakeholders — Due: 2025-01-20
transcript:
Meeting: Redwood Private (On-Prem/Air-Gapped) Technical Deep Dive — upgrades, rollback, offline bundles
Recorded: 2025-01-14 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Bruno Silva, Connor O'Brien, Marcus Lin
AsterPeak Financial Group: Priya Nair, Dan Wu, Elena Petrova, Tom Baird

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, we’re at the top of the hour. Thanks everyone for making time. Today we said we’d go deep on Private on-prem, especially upgrades and rollback, and how offline delivery works for air-gapped.

[00:12] Priya Nair: Yep. That’s the main blocker for us. We can handle the initial install, but ops is not signing up for a black box upgrade story.

[00:22] Markus Klein: Totally fair. Bruno’s going to walk through the operational flow, Connor can go into how the upgrade plan is computed, and Marcus can cover signing and audit.

[00:35] Bruno Silva: Hey all.

[00:36] Connor O'Brien: Hi.

[00:38] Marcus Lin: Hello.

[00:41] Dan Wu: Hey.

[00:43] Elena Petrova: Hi.

[00:45] Tom Baird: Afternoon.

[00:49] Markus Klein: Quick framing—this is Redwood Private, so dedicated control plane components in your cluster, and we ship upgrades as versioned bundles. We don’t assume any outbound internet. Priya, do you want to restate what “air-gapped” means in your environment? Like truly no egress at all?

[01:09] Priya Nair: Correct. No egress. We have an internal artifact repo. There is a manual process to import artifacts after security scans. Also, our change management requires a pre-approved maintenance window and evidence of what changed.

[01:25] Bruno Silva: Got it. That matches how a lot of banks do it.

[01:30] Dan Wu: And we need non-interactive execution. Like, we can have a human kick it off, but we can’t have “press y” prompts midstream in the run. If it needs confirmation, it needs to be a flag.

[01:43] Connor O'Brien: Yep, we have both modes. Interactive is default for safety in the CLI, but there’s a “--yes” / “--non-interactive” path plus explicit “--rollback-on-failure” behavior.

[01:56] Elena Petrova: Before we get too far, I want to understand the signing. Who holds keys, how do you rotate, how do we validate offline, and what do you log?

[02:06] Marcus Lin: Sure, we’ll cover that. The short version: bundles are signed, installer verifies signatures and hashes before it touches the cluster. We can support a model where Redwood signs release artifacts, and you import our public cert chain into your environment. Key rotation is handled by shipping overlapping trust for a period.

[02:28] Elena Petrova: Okay, but I’ll need details, not just a short version.

[02:31] Marcus Lin: Totally.

[02:33] Markus Klein: Bruno, do you want to start with the upgrade mechanics and the “maintenance window” question? Then we can zoom into signing and migrations.

[02:41] Bruno Silva: Yeah. So conceptually an upgrade run in Private is an orchestrated workflow. It has phases: prechecks, backup, staged apply, validation gates, and then “mark success.” If any gate fails we stop and either instruct a manual rollback or trigger an automated rollback if it’s still within a safe boundary.

[03:05] Dan Wu: What is “safe boundary” exactly?

[03:08] Connor O'Brien: The big one is database migrations. If a migration is tagged forward-only, we will not automatically roll back past it. The installer will block rollback and tell you why, unless you have a tested restore path from snapshot.

[03:23] Dan Wu: So then rollback is really “restore,” not rollback.

[03:27] Connor O'Brien: In that scenario, yes, the rollback involves restoring the control-plane DB snapshot and re-applying the previous chart versions.

[03:35] Priya Nair: That’s acceptable if it’s clearly documented and predictable.

[03:40] Bruno Silva: And the tooling is designed to make it predictable. There’s an “upgrade plan” output that shows the step graph—what will run, in which order, and what the gates are.

[03:52] Markus Klein: When we say “plan,” think like Terraform plan, but for the Redwood Private components.

[03:58] Tom Baird: Sorry, can I ask a procurement-ish question? Are these upgrades included, or is this a separate SKU? I know this is technical, but…

[04:07] Markus Klein: Fair question. Upgrades are part of the platform license/support. Some customers pay for extended support windows, but the mechanism is core.

[04:16] Tom Baird: OK.

[04:18] Bruno Silva: On maintenance window: for a typical medium deployment—say 3 control-plane nodes and, I don’t know, 8 GPU workers—the downtime is usually bounded by gateway restarts and any schema migration time. We aim for minimized downtime, but not “always zero.”

[04:37] Dan Wu: Give me a number. 15 minutes? 2 hours?

[04:41] Bruno Silva: If it’s a patch/minor upgrade with no heavy DB change, 20–40 minutes is typical. If there’s a large migration, it can be longer. That’s why prechecks include a migration preview step and we recommend you do a rehearsal in staging.

[04:59] Priya Nair: “Migration preview” meaning what, like you run it but don’t commit?

[05:04] Connor O'Brien: Not exactly. We can inspect migration metadata to tell you whether it’s forward-only and estimate risk. Some migrations we can run in a job with a timeout and a lock—if it exceeds window, we abort before proceeding to the next components.

[05:22] Dan Wu: So there is an abort?

[05:24] Connor O'Brien: Yes. Abort will stop at the current step and leave the system in the “pre-upgrade” version if we haven’t crossed an irreversible boundary. If we have, abort turns into “restore from snapshot” guidance.

[05:39] Elena Petrova: And where is that metadata stored? In the DB itself?

[05:43] Connor O'Brien: There’s a migrations metadata table and the chart includes annotations that indicate required minimum version and whether downgrade is supported.

[05:53] Bruno Silva: And from an operator perspective, the CLI output is explicit. It’ll say like “Rollback blocked: forward-only migration applied: 2025_01_10_add_policy_table” — I’m making up the name — and it’ll point to the restore step.

[06:12] Dan Wu: That’s good. But we need to test it. Our incident team will ask “prove it works.”

[06:19] Markus Klein: Yep. We usually do a failure-injection drill in staging during the pilot.

[06:25] Priya Nair: Let’s talk prechecks. What exactly gets checked? Because we’ve been burned by installers that check one thing and then fail on, like, some random RBAC permission halfway through.

[06:38] Connor O'Brien: Prechecks are pluggable checks with severity. Examples: Kubernetes version, node capacity, disk free on control-plane volumes, storage class availability, snapshot permissions, secret presence, and config drift detection.

[06:56] Dan Wu: Config drift how? You compare values.yaml?

[06:59] Connor O'Brien: Basically: we query the cluster resources and compare to what the installer expects for the current “known good” state, plus we check for manual modifications on critical objects.

[07:10] Bruno Silva: Also registry connectivity. In air-gapped, the “connectivity” is to your internal registry and your internal object store endpoint if you use one.

[07:19] Priya Nair: We don’t allow object store, it’s all on-prem storage.

[07:23] Bruno Silva: OK, then the backup mechanism would lean on PV snapshots and/or an external backup tool. We support a baseline: snapshot the control-plane database and back up config/state.

[07:36] Dan Wu: When you say “control-plane database,” what is it? Postgres?

[07:40] Connor O'Brien: Yes, Postgres for control-plane state.

[07:43] Dan Wu: Is it embedded or external?

[07:45] Bruno Silva: Both are possible. Many on-prem customers run it in-cluster with a StatefulSet, some use an external managed Postgres equivalent. The upgrade flow needs snapshot capability either way.

[07:57] Priya Nair: Our preference is external Postgres on hardened VMs.

[08:02] Connor O'Brien: That’s fine. In that case our backup “primitive” is: run a snapshot command (pg_dump or your snapshot API) and then verify it, and record the backup ID in the upgrade run log.

[08:17] Elena Petrova: What does “verify” mean? You attempt restore?

[08:21] Connor O'Brien: Verification step is usually: ensure the snapshot exists, ensure it’s readable, and optionally do a lightweight restore into a temp DB in staging. In prod during a window, we typically do “exists + integrity checks,” not a full restore.

[08:38] Dan Wu: We’ll want a restore drill quarterly anyway.

[08:41] Markus Klein: That’s consistent with what we recommend.

[08:45] Elena Petrova: Now artifact delivery. We have to scan images. We also need to see exactly what images you’re deploying and their hashes.

[08:54] Marcus Lin: The offline bundle includes a manifest listing every artifact: container images, Helm charts, the installer binary, and metadata like versions, digests (sha256), and signature. The installer can run in a “verify only” mode to validate signature chain and digests.

[09:14] Elena Petrova: Good. And the signing—do you sign the manifest or each artifact?

[09:19] Marcus Lin: We sign the manifest, and the manifest includes digests of each artifact. Some customers also want image-level signatures (like cosign) in addition; we can support that depending on your policy.

[09:32] Dan Wu: Are you calling it “co-sign” or “cosign”? (laughs)

[09:35] Marcus Lin: Cosign, sorry. The tool.

[09:38] Priya Nair: And then how do images get loaded? We don’t want the installer reaching out to some public registry.

[09:46] Bruno Silva: Right. For air-gapped, the operator imports the bundle to an internal registry. The installer then references images from that registry via values. There’s also a bundle “import” command that can push images into your registry.

[10:03] Dan Wu: Is that deterministic? Like it won’t tag “latest” or something.

[10:07] Connor O'Brien: No “latest.” Everything is pinned by digest.

[10:10] Dan Wu: Thank you.

[10:12] Elena Petrova: Key custody. If Redwood signs, what prevents a malicious insider from pushing a bad build?

[10:19] Marcus Lin: So we use a controlled release signing process. Keys are stored in an HSM-backed system. Access is limited. Each release includes provenance metadata—build IDs, git commit, and the signing event is auditable. In your environment, you trust only our public cert(s). If you want an additional control, you can require a second signature from your internal security team before import.

[10:46] Elena Petrova: That’s probably what we’ll do.

[10:48] Tom Baird: That aligns with our policy. Dual approval.

[10:52] Priya Nair: I want to circle back on rollback. If the gateway gets upgraded but the control plane doesn’t, can we end in a split-brain scenario?

[11:02] Connor O'Brien: The ordering is designed to avoid that. Control plane first, then runtime components, then gateways, then observability agents. And there are readiness gates so a gateway rollout doesn’t proceed if the control plane health endpoint isn’t reporting ready.

[11:18] Dan Wu: Is that enforced by Helm hooks or by the installer?

[11:21] Connor O'Brien: Both. The installer orchestrates steps and Helm hooks implement per-component gating jobs. So even if someone runs “helm upgrade” manually, the chart includes safeguards.

[11:35] Priya Nair: Good. We have people who do that.

[11:37] Bruno Silva: (laughs) We’ve seen it.

[11:40] Dan Wu: Okay, say upgrade fails mid-way—image pull fails because our registry is missing one image. What happens?

[11:50] Connor O'Brien: That’s precheckable; we can validate all required images exist in your registry before proceeding. If it still happens mid-run, the step fails, we stop, and we generate a diagnostics bundle. Rollback can re-apply previous versions if no irreversible steps were applied.

[12:10] Dan Wu: Diagnostics bundle includes what? Kubernetes events, logs?

[12:13] Bruno Silva: Yes: precheck report, step timing, recent pod logs for involved namespaces, relevant k8s events, and the upgrade correlation ID.

[12:23] Priya Nair: Correlation ID across services is huge. We need that for our logging.

[12:27] Connor O'Brien: We propagate that ID into control-plane logs as well.

[12:32] Elena Petrova: Are upgrade actions audit logged? Like who ran it, what version.

[12:37] Marcus Lin: Yes—upgrade start, upgrade end, rollback start, rollback end, target version, previous version, operator identity. If you integrate with your IDP, we can log the user identity. If it’s run as a service account, then it’s that account.

[12:56] Tom Baird: We’ll need that for compliance.

[12:58] Markus Klein: Makes sense.

[13:00] Priya Nair: Let’s get specific on maintenance windows. We typically get 2 hours once per month for this class of change, sometimes 4 hours quarterly. Can we guarantee completion?

[13:12] Bruno Silva: We can’t guarantee in all environments, but we can help bound it. For GA we’ll have targets for upgrade time and we’ll provide a pre-flight estimate based on your cluster size and whether migrations are present.

[13:26] Dan Wu: Do you do canaries? Like upgrade one gateway at a time.

[13:30] Connor O'Brien: Yes, for gateways and runtime nodes we can do staged rollouts. Control plane tends to be more atomic, but we do it with readiness checks and timeouts.

[13:43] Priya Nair: And what about “previous known good version” tracking? Like one-click rollback.

[13:49] Connor O'Brien: We store the “last successful” version in control-plane state and the installer reads it. So the rollback command can default to that version.

[13:59] Dan Wu: But if the DB is corrupted, you lose that.

[14:02] Connor O'Brien: True, which is why the installer also writes the run record locally and in a ConfigMap, and the backup snapshot ID is printed and recorded.

[14:15] Elena Petrova: Local record is risky, because if a laptop dies.

[14:18] Bruno Silva: Agreed. The record in-cluster plus your ticketing evidence is the primary.

[14:24] Markus Klein: Connor, can you describe the upgrade “plan” output? Priya asked for evidence and predictability.

[14:31] Connor O'Brien: Sure. Operator runs: “redwood-private upgrade plan --target 1.12.3” (example). It prints a step graph like:
- Step 1: Prechecks (k8s >= 1.27, disk >= 30GB, snapshot permissions)
- Step 2: Backup control-plane DB (snapshot + verify)
- Step 3: Apply control-plane chart
- Step 4: Wait for control-plane healthy
- Step 5: Run DB migrations job (with policy checks)
- Step 6: Apply runtime components
- Step 7: Apply gateway components
- Step 8: Post-upgrade smoke tests
And each has a rollback hook definition.

[15:10] Dan Wu: Is that output machine-readable?

[15:13] Connor O'Brien: Yes, JSON output is supported.

[15:17] Dan Wu: Perfect. We’ll ingest it into our change record.

[15:21] Priya Nair: What about version compatibility? We’ve had issues where chart version expects API version not present.

[15:28] Connor O'Brien: We enforce a compatibility matrix: control plane version, runtime version, and chart versions must be compatible. The precheck step calls the control plane to report current component versions and blocks invalid combos with explicit errors.

[15:47] Priya Nair: Okay.

[15:49] Elena Petrova: How does the installer talk to the control plane if the control plane is down?

[15:55] Bruno Silva: Then the installer can only do cluster-level checks, but not API-level checks. In that scenario, upgrade is blocked unless you pass an override, but we discourage that.

[16:07] Dan Wu: Good.

[16:09] Markus Klein: We should address offline bundle workflow end-to-end. Elena, does your team prefer “we hand you a tarball” or “you pull from a marketplace” is not an option, right?

[16:20] Elena Petrova: Not an option. We need an archive file. It goes through malware scan, SBOM checks, and then we import.

[16:29] Marcus Lin: We can provide an archive. It will include SBOMs as well.

[16:34] Elena Petrova: For each container?

[16:36] Marcus Lin: Yes—image SBOMs plus an overall bundle SBOM.

[16:42] Dan Wu: And the “import” process… is it a single command?

[16:46] Bruno Silva: Typically: 1) verify bundle, 2) import images to your registry, 3) run upgrade plan, 4) run upgrade apply.

[16:56] Dan Wu: If step 2 fails midway, can it resume?

[16:59] Bruno Silva: Yes, it’s idempotent—because it checks digests.

[17:05] Priya Nair: Now a tricky part: Our internal registry requires short-lived tokens. If upgrade takes long, pulls might fail.

[17:14] Connor O'Brien: That’s something we can plan for by ensuring nodes can pull with a node-level credential or imagePullSecrets that remain valid for the window. Precheck can validate secret presence and expiration if you encode it.

[17:31] Dan Wu: We can do that.

[17:33] Elena Petrova: How are secrets handled during backups? You said “config/state backup.” Does that include secrets?

[17:40] Bruno Silva: By default, we do not export Kubernetes secrets in plaintext. We back up references and non-sensitive config. If you want secret backup, it has to be integrated with your secrets manager.

[17:55] Elena Petrova: Good. We don’t want plaintext secrets in tarballs.

[17:59] Marcus Lin: Also the diagnostics bundle will redact known secret patterns and exclude secret resources.

[18:05] Dan Wu: “Known patterns” makes me nervous.

[18:08] Marcus Lin: Agreed. It’s defense in depth, not a guarantee. You can run diagnostics generation in a “safe mode” that excludes more.

[18:17] Priya Nair: Okay.

[18:19] Markus Klein: Dan, earlier you mentioned non-interactive. Any other automation constraints? Ansible? Jenkins?

[18:27] Dan Wu: We run Jenkins pipelines. We need exit codes and structured logs. Also we need to be able to pass a change ticket ID through.

[18:35] Connor O'Brien: Structured logs: yes. There’s a correlation ID and you can pass a “--metadata change_ticket=CHG-1234” and it’ll show up in audit logs and the run record.

[18:49] Dan Wu: Great.

[18:52] Priya Nair: Another thing: do you support blue/green? Like standing up new control plane, switching traffic.

[18:58] Bruno Silva: Not as a default mode today. Some customers do dual clusters for HA/DR, but in a single cluster it’s in-place upgrade.

[19:09] Priya Nair: Understood.

[19:11] Elena Petrova: Competitors… we’ve looked at NVIDIA NIM and just running vLLM ourselves. The gap is mostly ops and compliance. If we go with you, we need to be confident upgrades don’t become a quarterly fire drill.

[19:25] Markus Klein: That’s exactly what this project is about. We’re codifying the upgrade workflow and support playbooks.

[19:31] Dan Wu: What’s your stance on “downgrade”? Like, do you support going back two versions?

[19:37] Connor O'Brien: We support rollback within a defined window, typically to the “previous known good” version, assuming migrations allow it or you restore from snapshot. We do not promise arbitrary downgrades across major versions.

[19:54] Dan Wu: So if we go 1.12 to 1.13 and it’s bad, we can go back to 1.12 if we do it within the window.

[20:01] Connor O'Brien: Correct, with caveats on forward-only migrations.

[20:06] Priya Nair: What about “runtime only” upgrades? Like we keep control plane stable.

[20:11] Bruno Silva: We generally recommend upgrading as a bundle because compatibility matrix is tested that way. But there can be cases where runtime patch is allowed; the matrix would encode it.

[20:23] Dan Wu: Good.

[20:25] Elena Petrova: Logging again: do you emit to our SIEM? We use Splunk.

[20:30] Marcus Lin: You can ship audit logs to your sink. Many customers use fluentbit/OTel collector to forward.

[20:40] Priya Nair: Okay.

[20:42] Markus Klein: Let’s do a hypothetical upgrade and failure scenario, because that’s how ops will think. Dan, pick a failure.

[20:49] Dan Wu: Disk full on the control plane volume during backup.

[20:54] Connor O'Brien: Precheck includes disk space, but yes, it can still happen if something spikes. During backup step, if it fails, we abort before changing versions. The system remains on old version, and we emit remediation: free space, rerun backup.

[21:12] Dan Wu: Good. Next: schema mismatch. Like DB migration fails.

[21:18] Connor O'Brien: Migration step runs with a lock. If it fails, we stop. If migration partially applied, we determine whether it’s reversible. If not, we instruct restore from snapshot. The key thing: snapshot happens before migration.

[21:34] Priya Nair: So snapshot is mandatory.

[21:37] Bruno Silva: For on-prem, yes, we strongly recommend it and in many cases we’ll block the upgrade without it unless you pass an explicit “--no-backup” override which support will discourage.

[21:51] Tom Baird: Support will “discourage” meaning what? Contractually?

[21:55] Markus Klein: More like: not best practice; we’ll document support boundaries. But we can talk commercial terms separately.

[22:03] Tom Baird: Okay.

[22:05] Elena Petrova: About bundle signing again—if we store your public key, what happens on rotation? We can’t be surprised.

[22:12] Marcus Lin: Rotation is announced in advance. Bundles include signatures that chain to both old and new during transition. You update the trusted cert bundle once per rotation cadence. We can align with your quarterly window.

[22:28] Elena Petrova: And if verification fails, what’s the behavior? Hard stop?

[22:33] Marcus Lin: Hard stop. No apply. It prints the reason—expired cert, digest mismatch, unknown issuer.

[22:41] Dan Wu: That’s good. But ensure the error message is not “something went wrong.”

[22:45] Connor O'Brien: (laughs) Agreed.

[22:48] Priya Nair: Another operational concern: we want an “evidence packet” for each change. Plan output, what versions, what checks passed, and final status.

[22:58] Bruno Silva: The upgrade record includes: precheck report, plan, start/end timestamps, versions, backup IDs, and link to diagnostics bundle if any. We can export as JSON and you can attach to change ticket.

[23:16] Dan Wu: Can it generate a single tarball with all of that?

[23:19] Bruno Silva: Yes, that’s basically the diagnostics bundle.

[23:22] Priya Nair: Good.

[23:24] Markus Klein: We’re halfway through. Anything we didn’t hit? Maybe competitors aside, I want to be sure we cover the “what do you ship” question.

[23:33] Priya Nair: Yes—what exactly is in the offline bundle? Like is it just Helm charts or also the container images.

[23:41] Bruno Silva: Both. Installer binary, Helm charts, container images, and manifest. Optionally dashboards package if you deploy that in-cluster.

[23:54] Dan Wu: Do you include Kubernetes manifests or CRDs?

[23:58] Connor O'Brien: CRDs are included, yes. Managed through Helm.

[24:03] Elena Petrova: SBOMs included. Great.

[24:06] Dan Wu: How big is the bundle?

[24:09] Bruno Silva: Depends on models you include. Control plane + basic runtime is manageable, but model weights can be large. Many customers handle model artifacts separately. For upgrades, we try to keep it to software artifacts; weights are an add-on.

[24:25] Priya Nair: We will manage weights separately. We have a model registry.

[24:30] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[24:32] Dan Wu: Another question: Does the upgrade require draining GPU nodes?

[24:36] Bruno Silva: Not necessarily. Runtime upgrades may restart pods; you can configure disruption budgets. For strict uptime, you’d need enough capacity to roll.

[24:49] Dan Wu: Okay.

[24:51] Priya Nair: We can overprovision during the window.

[24:54] Connor O'Brien: Then you can do a safer rollout.

[24:58] Elena Petrova: What about network policies? Our cluster is locked down.

[25:03] Bruno Silva: Precheck includes connectivity within namespaces and required ports. We can provide a list of required flows.

[25:12] Dan Wu: That list is key.

[25:14] Markus Klein: We’ll send that.

[25:16] (crosstalk)

[25:17] Priya Nair: Sorry, can you clarify “rollback hooks per component”?

[25:22] Connor O'Brien: Each component has pre/post hooks. Example: before upgrading gateway, ensure control plane healthy. For rollback, gateway can be rolled back to previous chart version, and we run a pre-stop hook to reduce split-brain risk.

[25:40] Priya Nair: Okay.

[25:42] Dan Wu: Is rollback automatic?

[25:45] Bruno Silva: It can be configured. Default is “stop and ask” because in on-prem you might want human confirmation. But you can set auto-rollback for certain failures if within safe bounds.

[26:00] Dan Wu: We probably want auto-rollback in staging, manual in prod.

[26:05] Markus Klein: That’s common.

[26:07] Elena Petrova: If someone runs rollback, is that logged as an auditable action?

[26:12] Marcus Lin: Yes.

[26:13] Elena Petrova: Good.

[26:16] Tom Baird: I’m going to drop in a minute, but before I go—are there any special support terms needed for on-prem upgrades? Like do we need “premium support.”

[26:26] Markus Klein: Typically on-prem includes a defined support tier; premium can add faster response and guided upgrade windows. We can cover after the technical fit is confirmed.

[26:36] Tom Baird: OK. Thanks.

[26:38] (Tom Baird left the call)

[26:40] Priya Nair: Another nit: When you say “installer,” is it a container or binary.

[26:45] Bruno Silva: It’s a binary CLI, can also run in a container if you prefer. Air-gapped folks often prefer a binary that runs on a bastion.

[26:55] Dan Wu: We’ll do bastion.

[26:57] Elena Petrova: Bastion has strict controls, but OK.

[27:01] Connor O'Brien: The CLI produces consistent exit codes. That helps Jenkins.

[27:06] Dan Wu: Perfect.

[27:08] Priya Nair: Can we do a “verify only” that doesn’t talk to cluster? Like just verify signatures and digest.

[27:14] Marcus Lin: Yes—offline verification without cluster access.

[27:18] Priya Nair: Great.

[27:19] Dan Wu: And then a separate “precheck” that talks to cluster.

[27:22] Connor O'Brien: Exactly.

[27:24] Elena Petrova: I want to confirm: no secrets in backups, no secrets in diagnostics by default.

[27:30] Bruno Silva: Correct.

[27:32] Elena Petrova: OK.

[27:34] Markus Klein: I’m going to ask the “timeline” question. If we can answer these items, what’s your target for a pilot?

[27:42] Priya Nair: We’d like a lab install next month and a formal pilot in Q2. But only if we have the upgrade story documented.
